intro: Cat Tien National Park protects a great stretch of lowland forest and grassland in southern Vietnam, north-east of Ho Chi Minh City in Đồng Nai province. A reader sent us one of its giants: a tung tree whose fin-shaped buttress roots stand taller than a person, which they call the Thunder Lizard and put at more than 400 years old.

trees.how_to_recognise: Beside the forest trail: a pale grey trunk rising straight into the canopy from enormous fin-shaped buttress roots, taller than a person where they meet the trunk, spreading over a floor of dark stones.

trees.story:
The reader who sent us this tree from Cat Tien National Park, north-east of Ho Chi Minh City, calls it the Thunder Lizard, and the photograph shows why it needs a big name.

It is a tung, Tetrameles nudiflora, one of the giants of the lowland forests of South and South-East Asia, and its foot is the whole spectacle. Great buttress roots run out from the trunk like the fins of a rocket, taller than a person where they meet it and still knee-high metres away, before they sink into the stony forest floor. The visitor standing between two of them in the reader's picture comes barely a third of the way up. Above them the pale grey trunk rises straight into the canopy, far over the trees around it.

The reader puts it at more than 400 years old, and writes that it outlived the war, when bombing and defoliants destroyed much of the forest canopy in the region. Those are their words; we have not yet seen a source for this tree's age, and we would welcome one.

Walk the trail slowly as you come near, and look for the fins first.
